issues.legal_issue: A will is not presumed to have been duly executed and attested merely because it is more than thirty years old.
material_facts: The disputed will was more than thirty years old when it was relied on in the suit.
The beneficiaries relied on the document’s age to seek a presumption that it had been duly executed and attested.
issues.conclusion: The presumption for documents more than thirty years old does not establish due execution or attestation of a will; the will must be proved under the requirements applicable to wills.
issues.legal_principle: Section 90 of the Evidence Act does not create a presumption of due execution and attestation for a will. A will must be proved in accordance with Section 63(c) of the Succession Act read with Section 68 of the Evidence Act. The Court relied on Bharpur Singh v. Shamsher Singh.

predicates.will_proof_dispute: A party to a proceeding disputes whether a will was duly executed and proved.
predicates.will_is_more_than_thirty_years_old: The will relied on in the proceeding is more than thirty years old.

issues.definition: When a proceeding disputes proof of a will, the will's age alone does not produce a presumption of due execution.

issues.legal_issue: A will's attestation may be established by inference from the attesting witness's evidence and surrounding circumstances when the witness does not specifically recall every detail of attestation.
material_facts: One attesting witness testified that the testator signed the will in his presence and that he signed it in the testator's presence.
The witness identified the other attesting witness's signature and testified that the other witness, the testator and others were present while the will was being written.
The other attesting witness had died before the evidence was given.
The opposing party did not challenge in cross-examination the evidence that the other attesting witness was present when the will was executed.
The will was registered the day after its execution, and the evidence and surrounding circumstances supported the inference that both attesting witnesses attested it in the testator's presence.
issues.conclusion: The evidence, considered with the surrounding circumstances, established due attestation and execution of the will; the beneficiaries had proved the will.
issues.legal_principle: Section 63(c) of the Succession Act requires attestation by two or more witnesses, each of whom must see the testator sign or acknowledge the signature, and each of whom must sign in the testator's presence. Section 68 of the Evidence Act requires at least one available attesting witness to be called. Section 71 permits other evidence where an attesting witness denies or does not recollect execution, but does not excuse failure to call an available witness. The Court relied on R. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Smt. Jaswant Kaur v. Smt. Amrit Kaur and Janki Narayan Bhoir v. Narayan Namdeo Kadam. It also relied on the approach to inference from evidence and surrounding circumstances in A.E.G. Carapiet v. A.Y. Derderian and Mahalaxmi Bank Limited v. Kamkhyalal Goenka, and on the court's role in assessing a will described in Gurdev Kaur v. Kaki.

rule.if: will_proof_dispute and one_attesting_witness_testifies and other_attesting_witness_unavailable and (attesting_witness_does_not_recall_every_attestation_detail or attestation_details_are_omitted) and surrounding_evidence_supports_due_attestation

predicates.will_proof_dispute: A party to a proceeding disputes whether a will was duly executed and proved.
predicates.one_attesting_witness_testifies: The party relying on the will calls an attesting witness who gives evidence about its execution.
predicates.other_attesting_witness_unavailable: The other attesting witness cannot give evidence because that witness is unavailable.
predicates.attesting_witness_does_not_recall_every_: The testifying attesting witness does not remember every detail of how the other witness attested the will.
predicates.attestation_details_are_omitted: The testifying attesting witness's evidence omits a specific detail about the other witness's attestation.
predicates.surrounding_evidence_supports_due_attest: Other evidence and circumstances support the conclusion that the testator and both attesting witnesses were present and that the will was attested as required.

issues.definition: When one attesting witness testifies, the other is unavailable, and the witness's incomplete recollection or omitted details are supported by other evidence, due attestation may be inferred.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court may interfere in a second appeal with concurrent findings of fact when those findings are perverse because of non-consideration of relevant evidence or an erroneous approach to the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court concurrently found that the will had not been proved, based on their assessment of the attesting witness's evidence.
The High Court concluded that the lower courts had misread the evidence about the circumstances surrounding execution and found their conclusions perverse and contrary to the record.
The will's execution and construction, as the foundation of the claimed rights, were before the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was right to allow the second appeal because the concurrent findings were erroneous and perverse in light of the evidence; the appeal to the Supreme Court was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits a second appeal on a substantial question of law. The construction of a document of title or a document founding the parties' rights necessarily raises a question of law; whether a question is substantial depends on the case's circumstances. A second appeal may address fact findings where they are vitiated by non-consideration of relevant evidence or an erroneous approach and are perverse. The Court relied on Chunilal Mehta v. Century Spinning and Manufacturing Company, Santosh Hazari v. Purushottam Tiwari and Union of India v. Ibrahim Uddin; it distinguished the appellant's reliance on Narayanan Rajendran v. Lekshmy Sarojini.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from decisions of a trial court and a first appellate court.
predicates.concurrent_findings_of_fact: The lower courts reached the same factual finding.
predicates.findings_are_perverse_due_to_relevant_ev: The concurrent finding resulted from overlooking relevant evidence or assessing it through an erroneous approach, making the finding perverse.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, the High Court may interfere with concurrent factual findings when they are perverse because relevant evidence was overlooked or erroneously assessed.
